target.title: fix(google): Veo video generation fails with google-prefixed model ids
target.body:
Closes #103291

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where calling the Google video generation provider with a `google/`-prefixed Veo model id (e.g. `google/veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview`) sends the request to the invalid path `models/google/veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview:predictLongRunning`, producing an `API_KEY_INVALID`-style error instead of the correct `models/veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview:predictLongRunning` endpoint.

## Why This Change Was Made

The GenAI SDK treats any model id that does not start with `models/` or `tunedModels/` as `models/<input>`, so a bare `google/veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview` becomes `models/google/veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview`. The provider now normalizes Veo video model ids to the bare form before both the SDK call and the REST fallback, ensuring both paths hit `models/veo-...:predictLongRunning`.

## User Impact

Users can now use `google/veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview`, `google/models/veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview`, or `veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview` interchangeably for Google video generation.

## Evidence

### Shared-runtime regression

Added `src/video-generation/runtime.test.ts` regression verifying that the shared runtime strips the provider prefix from `google/veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview` and forwards the bare model id to the provider.

### Provider behavior proof (before / after)

Ran a temporary harness that exercises the real provider code path with a stubbed API key and intercepts the outgoing HTTP request. The URL below is exactly what the provider would send to Google.

**Before this change** (reverting `extensions/google/video-generation-provider.ts` to `HEAD~1`):
```text
[URL-PROOF] https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/google/veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview:predictLongRunning
```

**After this change** (current branch):
```text
[URL-PROOF] https://generativelanguage.googleapis.com/v1beta/models/veo-3.1-fast-generate-preview:predictLongRunning
```

The API key was redacted; no real Google account, private endpoint, IP, or project id appears in the output.

### Test / check output

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/google/video-generation-provider.test.ts` — 18 tests passed
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/video-generation/runtime.test.ts` — 29 tests passed
- `oxfmt` and `oxlint` clean on changed files

### Note on live API proof

I do not have a live Google API key available in this environment, so the before/after above uses the real provider code path with intercepted HTTP. If a maintainer can provide a redacted live run log, I am happy to append it.

target.title: fix(memory): filter heartbeat acks robustly in dreaming ingestion (#1…
target.body:
Related: #103720

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the dreaming (memory synthesis) ingestion pipeline
would leak assistant heartbeat acknowledgements into the dream corpus as
low-confidence (0.58) snippets. These snippets then dominated the Light
and REM dream phases, leaving the synthesis subagent unable to build a
meaningful narrative and producing unusable fallback entries ("A memory
trace surfaced, but details were unavailable in this run.") instead of
real dream content.

## Why This Change Was Made

The dreaming ingestion text sanitizer previously dropped only literal
`"HEARTBEAT_OK"` assistant replies, matching `normalized === HEARTBEAT_TOKEN`
exactly. It missed any acknowledgement wrapped in markup or carrying a
short status tail (e.g. `**HEARTBEAT_OK**` or `"3 unread emails.
HEARTBEAT_OK"`), so those leaked into the corpus.

This change reuses the shared, well-tested `isHeartbeatOkResponse` filter
(already used by `doctor-state-integrity` and `chat-display-projection`),
which handles markup stripping and token-bearing acks with a short tail via
the `ackMaxChars` budget. This replaces the brittle exact match so the
filtering path matches the other ingestion pipelines. Drops are decided on
the assistant side directly to avoid relying on cross-message coupling with
the preceding user message (which a user could spoof).

Design decisions and scope:

- **Issue 1 (deleted/reset transcripts being ingested) is deliberately out
  of scope.** The local `shouldSkipTranscriptFileForDreaming` intentionally
  retains `.jsonl.deleted.*` / `.jsonl.reset.*` files so that `memory_search`
  can still surface hits on post-reset/post-delete history (see #101322).
  Excluding them here would break that contract.
- **Known residual gap:** `isHeartbeatOkResponse` requires the literal
  `HEARTBEAT_OK` token to be present. Local models (oLLaMa/gemma, kimi)
  sometimes answer heartbeats in natural language without emitting the
  token; those remain unfiltered here and would need a cross-message
  heuristic (which conflicts with the anti-spoofing concern from the
  original report). Flagged for upstream discussion rather than silently
  partial-fixing.

## User Impact

When the model emits a heartbeat reply carrying the `HEARTBEAT_OK` token —
even wrapped in markup or with a short tail — dreaming ingestion now drops
it instead of ingesting it as dream content. The result is cleaner dream
phases and fewer unusable fallback entries. Real conversation content is
unaffected (the filter only drops when the token is present and the
remaining text falls within the acknowledgement budget).

## Evidence

- `isHeartbeatOkResponse` is an existing helper with unit-test coverage
  (`src/auto-reply/heartbeat-filter.test.ts`); its `shouldSkip === true`
  cases all cover token-bearing acks (plain, markup-wrapped, with a
  status prefix).
- Code review confirms: the change reuses a verified path rather than
  introducing new filtering logic; the unused `HEARTBEAT_TOKEN` import was
  removed to keep the tree clean; the re-export in `openclaw-runtime.ts`
  follows the existing passthrough pattern (`isHeartbeatUserMessage` and
  others are already re-exported from the same module).
- ⚠️ **Local tests/typecheck were not run** — `node_modules` is not
  installed in this checkout. Targets to run after `pnpm install`:
  `packages/memory-host-sdk/src/host/session-files.test.ts` (sanitizer)
  and `src/auto-reply/heartbeat-filter.test.ts` (helper). The existing
  `HEARTBEAT_OK` cases in the sanitizer tests should still pass (token
  case drops identically); markup-wrapped / tail acks should now also be
  dropped, given `isHeartbeatOkResponse` handles them.

target.title: fix(models): preserve static provider catalog metadata
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Static provider catalog conversion did not preserve all provider/model metadata consistently. The concrete current-main gap is provider-level `params`: static-catalog rows can define provider request params, but the returned runtime model did not merge those provider params with model params.

This PR also makes the static provider catalog converter explicitly carry `compat` and `mediaInput` so the returned runtime model preserves the same schema-valid metadata downstream payload and capability code expects.

## Why This Change Was Made

The runtime should preserve schema-valid provider/model metadata when resolving static provider catalog models. This is a metadata-propagation fix in `modelFromProviderStaticCatalog`; it does not add a new config key, policy path, transport, or custom-provider tool API.

Reviewer scope:
- This PR proves static provider catalog params/metadata propagation into the resolved runtime model and OpenAI-compatible request params via production modules.
- This PR is intentionally scoped away from the separate live-session `Tool exec not found` issue.
- Current main already keeps normal configured-provider compat flowing in other paths, and tools are permissive unless `compat.supportsTools === false`; the changed path here is static provider catalog conversion.

## User Impact

Users and bundled/provider catalogs can define provider-level request params and model metadata without losing that metadata during static provider catalog model resolution. Downstream payload generation and capability checks then receive the resolved model shape consistently.

## Evidence

Behavior or issue addressed:
- Static provider catalog conversion merges provider-level and model-level `params`, with model-level values taking precedence.
- Static provider catalog conversion preserves model `compat` metadata.
- Static provider catalog conversion preserves model `mediaInput` metadata.
- Live CLI proof shows `openclaw models list --all --provider cohere --json` resolving a real bundled static catalog row.
- Production helper proof shows resolved static-catalog `compat` metadata reaching `supportsModelTools(model)` and `buildOpenAICompletionsParams(...)` request shaping.
- Regression coverage verifies OpenAI completions payload construction respects resolved model metadata.

target.title: fix: keep native harness bridge tool caps local
target.body:
Closes #100988

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running a native CLI-harness parent session could spawn an embedded subagent that lost coding tools such as `read`, `write`, `exec`, `apply_patch`, and `process` because the parent bridge-visible OpenClaw tool list was persisted as the child session's inherited allowlist.

## Why This Change Was Made

Runtime tool allowlists are now local tool-surface materialization hints by default, so native harness bridge allowlists can still build/filter the tools exposed over the bridge without being persisted onto spawned child sessions. Embedded runtime `toolsAllow` remains opt-in inherited parent capability and is applied before the inherited tool surface is captured, preserving the non-escalation boundary for genuinely restricted parent runs.

## User Impact

CLI-harness parent sessions can delegate to embedded coding subagents without accidentally clamping those children to only gateway bridge tools. Explicit configured tool policies, inherited child policies, and embedded runtime `toolsAllow` restrictions still constrain spawned sessions.

## Evidence

AI-assisted PR.

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/agent-tools.create-openclaw-coding-tools.test.ts`
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/conversation-capability-profile.test.ts`
- `pnpm exec oxfmt --check --threads=1 src/agents/conversation-capability-profile.ts src/agents/agent-tools.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts src/agents/conversation-capability-profile.test.ts src/agents/agent-tools.create-openclaw-coding-tools.test.ts`
- `pnpm exec oxlint src/agents/conversation-capability-profile.ts src/agents/agent-tools.ts src/agents/embedded-agent-runner/run/attempt.ts src/agents/conversation-capability-profile.test.ts src/agents/agent-tools.create-openclaw-coding-tools.test.ts`
- `git diff --check`
- `.agents/skills/autoreview/scripts/autoreview --mode local` -> `autoreview clean: no accepted/actionable findings reported`


### Real Behavior Proof

Current head: `607b147b5878b6b5cbc414a0e9375ce84c025173`.

A temporary stdin `pnpm exec tsx` harness imported production `resolveConversationCapabilityProfile` and `spawnSubagentDirect`, simulated a native CLI-harness parent bridge allowlist, stubbed only gateway/session-store side effects, and inspected the child session patch that `sessions_spawn` persists.

```json
profile_policy {"bridgeExplicitAllowIncludesSessionsSpawn":true,"bridgeInheritanceAllowPolicies":[],"embeddedInheritanceAllowPolicies":[["sessions_spawn","read","exec"]]}
child_session_patch {"status":"accepted","childKeyShape":true,"gatewayMethods":["agent"],"inheritedToolAllow":null,"inheritedAllowClampsCodingTools":false}
```

This proves the native bridge allowlist remains local to parent tool materialization, is not stored as child `inheritedToolAllow`, and explicit embedded runtime `toolsAllow` remains opt-in inheritable for restricted-parent non-escalation.

target.title: fix(gateway): reconcile on-disk config after watcher recreate (#103729)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The gateway watches `openclaw.json` for hot-reload. When that watcher hits an error (for example EMFILE/ENOSPC inotify exhaustion) it is closed and re-created after a backoff. The re-created watcher is built with `ignoreInitial: true` and no reconciliation read, so any config edit made by an **external process** during the watcher-down window — a manual edit, or a separate `openclaw doctor --fix` run, neither of which routes through the running gateway's in-process write channel — is silently adopted as the new watcher's baseline and **never scheduled for reload**. The gateway keeps running the stale pre-edit config indefinitely, with no log distinguishing a missed change from a normal quiet period. This is exactly the population the inotify-exhaustion retries exist to serve.

Closes #103729

## Why This Change Was Made

`ignoreInitial: true` is correct for the very first watcher (startup already reads and applies the config). On **recreation**, however, there is an interval with no live watcher during which an on-disk change can occur, and the new watcher's `ignoreInitial: true` guarantees that change produces no event. Both recreate paths share the defect: the native-retry timer and the polling-degrade timer.

## Changes

- `createWatcher` gains an optional `reconcile` parameter. When `true`, after the fresh watcher is live it schedules one reconcile read (`scheduleAfter(0)`) against the current on-disk config through the existing scheduler — the canonical seam that owns snapshot reads, validation, diffing, and application.
- Both recreate timers (native-retry and polling-degrade) now call `createWatcher(true)`. The initial startup `createWatcher()` is unchanged, since startup already read and applied the config before the first watcher existed.
- Two regression tests cover both recreate paths.

## User Impact

External config edits (manual, or `openclaw doctor --fix`) that land while the watcher is recovering from an inotify/EMFILE error are now applied after the watcher is re-created, instead of being silently dropped until some later unrelated write touches the file again.

## Evidence

**Real behavior proof.** Drove the real `startGatewayConfigReloader` against a real on-disk `openclaw.json` with a real chokidar watcher. A real `error` event was emitted on the live watcher instance (as inotify exhaustion would raise it); the watcher, the file, the debounce/reload loop, and `readSnapshot` reading the file all stayed real. Edits: v2 while up, v3 during the recreate backoff window, v4 after the fresh watcher is live. Counted reload reads per edit and recorded which file contents were ever read.

```
# BEFORE (origin/main, buggy)
watchers_created=2
config_reads_after_up_edit(v2)=1
config_reads_after_downwindow_edit(v3)=0
config_reads_after_recreate_edit(v4)=1
v3_ever_read=false
raw_config_contents_read=["{\"v\":2}","{\"v\":4}"]   # v3 silently dropped

# AFTER (this PR, identical inputs)
watchers_created=2
config_reads_after_up_edit(v2)=1
config_reads_after_downwindow_edit(v3)=1              # reconcile read picks up v3
config_reads_after_recreate_edit(v4)=1
v3_ever_read=true
raw_config_contents_read=["{\"v\":2}","{\"v\":3}","{\"v\":4}"]
```

**Focused tests.** Two new tests in `config-reload.test.ts` assert a reconcile read runs after both recreate paths (native retry + polling degrade). Full suite green:

```
$ npx vitest run src/gateway/config-reload.test.ts
 Test Files  3 passed (3)
      Tests  267 passed (267)
```

target.title: test: cover ClickClack tail cursor fallback
target.body:
Related: #102486
Related: openclaw/clickclack#46

## What

Tests-only follow-up to #102486. Adds regression coverage for two ClickClack startup paths:

1. Gateway falls back to the last startup page cursor when the server omits `tail_cursor`
2. HTTP client drops non-string `tail_cursor` values (defensive guard for malformed responses)

No production code changes.

## Why

The merged #102486 implementation depends on a server-captured `tail_cursor`, with an old-server fallback when that field is absent. These tests lock both paths so future edits cannot quietly reopen startup backlog replay.

AI-assisted. Authored by ragesaq; code by Chisel; model `openai/gpt-5.5`.

## Real Behavior Proof

### Proof 1: ClickClack-stock omits `tail_cursor`

Live call against our running ClickClack-stock instance (`:8100`), which does NOT implement `tail_cursor`:

```
GET /api/realtime/events?workspace_id=wsp_01ktq4zg9a9cj7bhah8fqnmcya&include_tail=true&limit=2

Response:
{
  "events": [
    { "cursor": "cur_01ktxqf9dczwhfw9mbxmfengga", "type": "message.updated", "seq": 1518 },
    { "cursor": "cur_01ktxqg0m56r97b77kv3cedx7t", "type": "message.created", "seq": 1519 }
  ]
}
```

**`tail_cursor`: ABSENT.** The gateway must fall back to the last event cursor (`cur_01ktxqg0m56r97b77kv3cedx7t`). This is exactly the path the new gateway test covers.

### Proof 2: HTTP client drops non-string `tail_cursor`

Exercised the production `createClickClackClient.eventPage()` against a mock server returning `tail_cursor: 123` (numeric):

```
Mock server returned: { events: [...], tail_cursor: 123 }
Client parsed result: { events: [{ id: "evt-1", cursor: "cursor-1" }] }

PASS: tailCursor omitted - typeof guard at http-client.ts:126 works
```

Positive control (string `tail_cursor: "cursor-tail-42"`): correctly preserved as `tailCursor` in the result.

### Proof 3: Server source confirms

ClickClack-stock `listEvents` handler at `server.go:833`:
```go
writeResult(w, map[string]any{"events": events}, err)
```
No `tail_cursor` field emitted. The `include_tail` query param is accepted but not used (older server). This is the production server our fleet runs against.

## Validation

```
pnpm test:extension clickclack → 64/64 passed (8 files)
pnpm tsgo:extensions → passed
pnpm check:bundled-channel-config-metadata → passed
git diff --check → clean
```

`codex review` blocked locally (CLI auth 401). No production code changed.

Anvil mutation-checked both tests (RED-on-broken): mutating fallback logic or typeof guard failed exactly the corresponding new test, confirming both are load-bearing.

target.title: feat(agents): derive a provider-declared default utility model when unset
target.body:
Closes #103768. Follow-up to #103463 / #103461.

## What Problem This Solves

`utilityModel` (titles, progress narration) is opt-in config, so most installs pay primary-model prices for internal one-shots and never get narration. We already know from the agent's primary provider which vendor the user can call — and each major vendor ships a tiny model for exactly this.

## Why This Change Was Made

- **Provider-declared defaults, no ids in core.** New manifest field `modelCatalog.providers.<id>.defaultUtilityModel` (typed + normalized in `@openclaw/model-catalog-core`), mirroring the `mediaUnderstandingProviderMetadata.defaultModels` pattern. Seeded: OpenAI → `gpt-5.6-luna` (cheapest current-gen), Anthropic → `claude-haiku-4-5`. Google deferred (its catalog lives in plugin TS, not the manifest `providers` record).
- **Derivation follows the primary provider** (`src/agents/utility-model.ts`): unset `utilityModel` resolves the primary provider's declared default via the process-current plugin metadata snapshot — synchronous, cached, no probing or extra model calls; auth is inherent because the agent already runs on that provider. Explicit `utilityModel` wins; `utilityModel: ""` (agent- or defaults-level) disables utility routing entirely (titles → primary, narration off).
- **Narration auto-activates** when a default resolves (`attachProgressNarratorToReplyOptions` now gates on the shared resolver) and still never falls back to the primary model.
- **Transport fix (live-test finding):** the GPT-5.6 family rejects `temperature` with a 400 on the Responses API while 5.5/5.4 accept it — utility callers send `temperature: 0.3`, so the derived default would have failed every call. `supportsOpenAITemperature` (catalog `compat.supportsTemperature` override + family fallback, declared for all four gpt-5.6 manifest entries) now gates all three OpenAI payload builders (responses, shared, chatgpt-responses).

## User Impact

- OpenAI/Anthropic users get cheap titles and live progress narration with zero config; other providers keep exactly today's behavior (titles → primary, narration off) until they declare a default or set `utilityModel`.
- New opt-out: `utilityModel: ""`. Docs updated: `docs/gateway/config-agents.md`, `docs/concepts/models.md`, `docs/concepts/progress-drafts.md`, `docs/plugins/manifest.md` (new provider field).
- Existing explicit `utilityModel` configs behave identically.

## Evidence

- Live proof on Testbox against real APIs: `openai/gpt-5.6-luna` completes with temperature requested-but-stripped (reproduced the 400 without the fix), `openai/gpt-5.5` keeps temperature, `anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5` completes with real auth (all `stopReason=stop` with sensible status text).
- Testbox gates green at head: oxfmt, targeted oxlint, `plugins:inventory:check`, `docs:map:check`, `check:import-cycles`, `check:test-types`, and test files: `src/agents/utility-model.test.ts` (new), `simple-completion-runtime.selection.test.ts`, `progress-narrator.test.ts`, `model-catalog-normalize.test.ts`, `openai-reasoning-effort.test.ts`, `openai-responses-shared.test.ts`, `test/scripts/plugin-sdk-surface-report.test.ts`.
- New tests: setting parsing (unset/auto vs `""` disable vs explicit, agent-level override), provider-default derivation from injected snapshots, primary-provider derivation, empty-utility selection fallback, narration gating both directions, catalog normalization passthrough, temperature family/compat matrix, payload-builder temperature drop/keep.

target.title: fix(agent-tools): add request timeout to remote media fetches
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The agent-side image, image-generation, and PDF tools fetch remote media through `loadWebMediaRaw` with only a body-idle gap guard (`readIdleTimeoutMs`). A remote endpoint that accepts the TCP connection but withholds response headers forever leaves the fetch open indefinitely — `readIdleTimeoutMs` only governs gaps between body chunks, never the pre-header stall. This PR bounds that case with a total-request lifetime (overall `timeoutMs`) forwarded through the shared `WebMediaOptions` seam.

## Why This Change Was Made

- Aligns the three agent-tool callers to the **15-minute bounded-media ceiling** from canonical precedent #103266 (`src/cli/nodes-camera.ts:20`, `CAMERA_URL_DOWNLOAD_TIMEOUT_MS = 15 * 60_000`).
- Reuses the shared `WebMediaOptions.timeoutMs` seam from #103206 so the timeout is enforced by the same `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` mechanism used by other bounded fetchers. `readIdleTimeoutMs` (body-gap) stays separate and tighter.
- Both `timeoutMs` and `readIdleTimeoutMs` are forwarded together; slow-but-progressing transfers are still bounded by the body-idle guard, while a never-responding endpoint is now aborted at the overall deadline.

## What Changed

- `src/media/web-media.ts` — adds optional `timeoutMs?: number` to `WebMediaOptions` (after `readIdleTimeoutMs`) and forwards it through to `readRemoteMediaBuffer` / `fetchGuardedMediaResponse` / `fetchWithSsrFGuard` / `buildTimeoutAbortSignal`.
- `src/agents/tools/media-tool-shared.ts` — exports `REMOTE_MEDIA_TIMEOUT_MS = 15 * 60_000` next to the existing `REMOTE_MEDIA_READ_IDLE_TIMEOUT_MS`.
- `src/agents/tools/image-tool.ts`, `image-generate-tool.ts`, `pdf-tool.ts` — add `timeoutMs: REMOTE_MEDIA_TIMEOUT_MS` to the `loadWebMediaRaw` options for HTTP URLs (only when the reference is an `http(s)` URL; local/file paths are untouched).
- `src/agents/tools/{image,image-generate,pdf}-tool.test.ts` — assert the new `timeoutMs: 15 * 60_000` forwarding.
- `src/media/web-media.test.ts` — adds a **real-HTTP-server proof test** (below) that starts a Node.js HTTP server, withholds response headers, calls `loadWebMediaRaw` with the same options the agent tools forward, and asserts on the specific `MediaFetchError` / `TimeoutError` shape that surfaces to the tool layer.

## User Impact

- Image, image-generation, and PDF tool calls against stalled remote endpoints now abort at 15 minutes instead of running indefinitely. Behavior on normal-speed transfers is unchanged because `readIdleTimeoutMs` still fires first for slow-but-progressing body chunks.
- Slow transfers that genuinely exceed 15 minutes will now fail intentionally — this is the documented bounded-media contract.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof (real HTTP server, real fetch, real AbortSignal, surfaced error shape)

Added in `src/media/web-media.test.ts > aborts a real stalled HTTP server via the overall timeoutMs deadline`. This test starts an actual Node.js `http.createServer` that accepts the connection but never calls `res.writeHead`/`res.end`, then calls `loadWebMediaRaw` against `http://127.0.0.1:<port>/photo.png` using the **default `fetch`** (no `fetchImpl` override) with `timeoutMs = 400ms` and `readIdleTimeoutMs = 30_000ms` — the same forwarding shape the image/pdf/image-generate tools use. The test asserts:

1. The promise rejects (timeout fires).
2. Elapsed wall time is ≥ `timeoutMs - 50ms` (proves the wait happened) and < `timeoutMs + 5s` (proves it didn't fall back to the 15-min default).
3. The surfaced error has the exact shape the agent-tool layer will propagate: `MediaFetchError` with `code: "fetch_failed"`, `message: "Failed to fetch media from <url>: request timed out"`, and `cause: TimeoutError("request timed out")`.

Focused suite run (local fallback — Crabbox unavailable in this env):

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs run src/media/web-media.test.ts --reporter=verbose
…
 ✓ |media| src/media/web-media.test.ts > loadWebMedia > aborts a real stalled HTTP server via the overall timeoutMs deadline 425ms
 ✓ |media| src/media/web-media.test.ts > loadWebMedia > applies the shared remote read idle timeout for raw web media loads 22ms
 ✓ |media| src/media/web-media.test.ts > loadWebMedia > loads a valid remote PDF when the raw web media read stays active 5ms
…

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  76 passed (76)
   Start at  23:25:48
   Duration  3.55s
```

Surfaced error captured from the test (this is what the agent-tool layer receives and propagates to its caller):

```json
{
  "name": "MediaFetchError",
  "code": "fetch_failed",
  "message": "Failed to fetch media from http://127.0.0.1:46291/photo.png: request timed out",
  "cause": {
    "name": "TimeoutError",
    "message": "request timed out"
  }
}
```

The 425ms elapsed time for the `400ms` `timeoutMs` test confirms the AbortSignal fires at the deadline through the full production path (`loadWebMediaRaw` → `readRemoteMediaBuffer` → `fetchGuardedMediaResponse` → `fetchWithSsrFGuard` → `buildTimeoutAbortSignal` → `init.signal` → `globalThis.fetch`), not via a mocked rejection. The `MediaFetchError` with `TimeoutError` cause is the same error the image/pdf/image-generate tool `execute` functions will throw when the underlying fetch stalls, which means the agent runtime will surface a clean "request timed out" error to the caller instead of hanging.

### Canonical precedent

Merged #103266 (`src/cli/nodes-camera.ts:20`) established `15 * 60_000` as the bounded-media total-request lifetime for the "server never responds" stall class. This PR aligns the three agent-tool callers to the same ceiling.

### Tool-forwarding coverage

The three agent-tool test files now assert `timeoutMs: 15 * 60_000` forwarding alongside the existing `readIdleTimeoutMs` assertions:

- `src/agents/tools/image-tool.test.ts:2259`
- `src/agents/tools/image-generate-tool.test.ts`
- `src/agents/tools/pdf-tool.test.ts`

### Coordination with #103206

Both #103206 and this PR add the shared `WebMediaOptions.timeoutMs` seam because cross-repo fork PRs cannot stack on each other's fork branches — each must typecheck standalone. The intent is for #103206 to land first (it owns the seam + Tlon), then this PR reduces to the three agent-tool callers. The seam itself is identical (optional `timeoutMs?: number` after `readIdleTimeoutMs`, forwarded through `readRemoteMediaBuffer`).

target.title: fix(clickclack): strip internal tool-trace banners from outbound text
target.body:
Related: #90684

## What Problem This Solves

Assistant internal tool-trace scaffolding — `<tool_call>`-style XML blocks and `⚠️ 🛠️ … failed` tool banners, among the forms `sanitizeAssistantVisibleText()` strips — leaks verbatim into ClickClack chat whenever it appears in the assistant's reply text.

`sanitizeAssistantVisibleText()` exists for exactly this, but ClickClack's reply never runs it: the channel's inbound turn delivers through a custom `delivery.deliver` callback (`extensions/clickclack/src/inbound.ts`) that forwards `payload.text` straight to `sendClickClackText`. ClickClack declares no durable delivery route, so the channel turn kernel always takes that custom callback and never reaches the core-outbound `sanitizeText` normalization pass. An `outbound.base.sanitizeText` hook would sit on a boundary this reply path does not cross.

## Why This Change Was Made

This is the ClickClack sibling of the per-channel tool-trace fixes tracked under #90684. The other bundled chat adapters in this family (for example Twitch) reach the shared sanitizer because their inbound delivery declares a durable route, so the kernel runs the durable-first path where the core-outbound hook fires; their custom `deliver` is only a fallback. ClickClack has no durable route, so the equivalent fix has to live where its text actually leaves the process.

`sendClickClackText` is the single sender chokepoint every ClickClack delivery path funnels through — the inbound reply callback, the plain model-reply mode, the channel send adapter, and proactive outbound. Sanitizing there strips the scaffolding once for all of them and cannot be bypassed by a delivery path that skips the core hook:

```ts
const text = sanitizeAssistantVisibleText(params.text);
if (!text.trim()) {
  return { to: params.to };
}
```

A reply that is entirely scaffolding sanitizes to nothing. ClickClack rejects empty message bodies, and core outbound delivery likewise drops payloads emptied during normalization, so the sender suppresses the transport call and reports no message id rather than issuing a request the server refuses. The removed `outbound.base.sanitizeText` hook would have been redundant with this and is not added.

## User Impact

ClickClack users no longer see internal tool-call XML or tool-failure banners in chat when a model leaks scaffolding into its reply text. A reply that is nothing but scaffolding sends nothing at all, instead of a rejected empty request. Ordinary assistant prose is delivered unchanged. No config, schema, or API changes.

## Evidence

Real-path capture drives the production `sendClickClackText` against a local ClickClack HTTP server under `node --import tsx` and records the exact message body that reaches the wire — the same POST ClickClack's inbound `delivery.deliver` callback makes. No sanitizer, adapter, or transport code is faked; only the remote server is local. Captured against upstream `main` (before) and this PR's HEAD (after):

```
target                 input                                              before (main)              after (this PR)
channel quote-reply    "Done.\n⚠️ 🛠️ `search repos (agent)` failed"       reaches wire verbatim      "Done."
thread reply           "Done.\n⚠️ 🛠️ `search repos (agent)` failed"       reaches wire verbatim      "Done."
direct message         "<tool_call>{...}</tool_call>Deploy finished."     reaches wire verbatim      "Deploy finished."
all-scaffolding reply  "⚠️ 🛠️ `search repos (agent)` failed"              reaches wire verbatim      no request sent (no message id)
```

Focused regression tests (`extensions/clickclack/src/outbound-tool-trace-sanitize.test.ts`, 5 cases) assert the text handed to the HTTP client for each delivery kind (channel quote-reply, thread reply, direct message) is sanitized, that ordinary prose is preserved, and that an all-scaffolding reply issues no transport call and returns no message id. They exercise the real `sendClickClackText`; only the transport client is mocked.

Local (worktree at this PR's HEAD):

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/clickclack/src/outbound-tool-trace-sanitize.test.ts` — 5/5
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/clickclack` — 67/67
- `oxfmt` / `scripts/run-oxlint.mjs` on the touched files — clean
- `pnpm tsgo:extensions` — clean

`check:changed` lanes run on CI.

target.title: refactor(auth): harden CLI forwarding proposal boundary
target.body:
## Summary

Hardens the proposed CLI backend auth-forwarding boundary while keeping it internal and draft-only.

This remains separate from #99733 and #103715. It does not alter current CLI execution behavior and does not publish an incomplete Plugin SDK contract.

## What changed

- Rejects credential-provider mismatches before any resolver is invoked.
- Rejects credential-profile mismatches before any resolver is invoked.
- Replaces the open-ended raw credential record with closed selection metadata.
- Replaces the open-ended returned record with a closed execution envelope containing only identity, environment additions, and environment removals.
- Keeps the helper internal by removing the premature `openclaw/plugin-sdk/cli-backend` export.
- Preserves fail-closed handling for unsupported backends, denied providers, denied credential kinds, missing resolvers, explicit declines, and resolver output substitution.

## Security boundary

Canonical auth-profile secrets do not cross into the resolver input. The resolver receives validated provider, profile, model, backend, and credential-kind metadata only.

The resolver output must remain bound to the selected provider, profile, and credential kind. Cross-provider or cross-profile input is rejected before callback invocation, and output substitution throws.

## Current scope

This draft adds an internal validator and focused tests only.

It deliberately does not yet:

- add fields to `CliBackendPlugin`
- add a resolver hook to `ProviderPlugin`
- wire forwarding into CLI execution
- export a public Plugin SDK API
- claim live runtime behavior

A complete runtime consumer, documentation, SDK baseline, and security-owner approval should be reviewed together before any public contract is introduced.

## Validation

Focused coverage includes:

- explicit opt-in
- pre-resolver provider mismatch rejection
- pre-resolver profile mismatch rejection
- provider and credential-kind denial
- resolver absence and explicit decline
- closed-envelope forwarding
- resolver output provider, profile, and kind substitution rejection

Fresh CI is running on the current head.

## Tests

AI-assisted: yes.

target.title: fix(install-cli): track mktemp paths and clean up on EXIT
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`scripts/install-cli.sh` creates temporary directories and files during Node
install and pnpm workspace rewrites, but had no EXIT trap. On failure paths
(download error, shasum mismatch, early `fail`/`exit`), those paths were left
under `/tmp` until OS cleanup.

`scripts/install.sh` already tracks temps with `TMPFILES` and
`trap cleanup_tmpfiles EXIT`. This change brings `install-cli.sh` in line,
using caller-side registration (`tmp="$(mktemp -d)"; TMPFILES+=("$tmp")`)
because bash command-substitution helpers cannot mutate the parent array.

## Summary

- Add `TMPFILES` + `cleanup_tmpfiles` + `trap ... EXIT`
- Register the Node install temp dir and the pnpm workspace rewrite temp file
- Avoid `tmp="$(helper)"` registration helpers (subshell drops array updates)

## Change

```bash
TMPFILES=()
cleanup_tmpfiles() { ... }
trap cleanup_tmpfiles EXIT

tmp="$(mktemp -d)"
TMPFILES+=("$tmp")
# ... on any exit, trap removes registered paths
```

## Failure scenario

1. `install-cli.sh` starts Node user-space install → `mktemp -d`
2. Download or shasum check fails → `fail` / `exit`
3. Without the trap, the temp dir remains under `/tmp`

## Evidence

Terminal before/after on the same host (macOS, bash 5.3). Helpers mirror the
production registration pattern from this PR.

**Before (bare mktemp, no trap):** temp dir still exists after `exit 1`.

```console
$ bash /tmp/prove-before.sh
created temp dir: /var/folders/.../T/tmp.NoQGp8tzgN
simulating fail/exit 1...
BEFORE_PATCH: LEAKED path=/var/folders/.../T/tmp.NoQGp8tzgN
```

**After (TMPFILES register + EXIT trap):** temp dir removed on exit.

```console
$ bash /tmp/prove-after.sh
created temp dir: /var/folders/.../T/tmp.GaAkuJenu8
TMPFILES=/var/folders/.../T/tmp.GaAkuJenu8
exists before fail? yes
simulating fail/exit 1...
AFTER_PATCH: cleaned path=/var/folders/.../T/tmp.GaAkuJenu8
```

Production wiring in `scripts/install-cli.sh`:

```console
$ rg -n 'TMPFILES|trap cleanup_tmpfiles|mktemp' scripts/install-cli.sh | head
35:TMPFILES=()
42:trap cleanup_tmpfiles EXIT
846:  tmp="$(mktemp -d)"
847:  TMPFILES+=("$tmp")
1083:    tmp="$(mktemp)"
1084:    TMPFILES+=("$tmp")

$ bash -n scripts/install-cli.sh && shellcheck scripts/install-cli.sh
bash -n OK
shellcheck OK
```

## Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** install-cli temp dirs/files leaked on fail/exit because bare mktemp had no EXIT cleanup; command-substitution helpers also failed to register paths due to bash subshells.
- **Real environment tested:** macOS 15, bash 5.3.15 (Homebrew), shellcheck, branch `fix/install-cli-tmpfile-cleanup` at current HEAD.
- **Exact steps or command run after this patch:**

  ```bash
  # After-pattern (matches production registration)
  tmp="$(mktemp -d)"; TMPFILES+=("$tmp"); exit 1
  # Before-pattern
  tmp="$(mktemp -d)"; exit 1
  bash -n scripts/install-cli.sh
  shellcheck scripts/install-cli.sh
  ```

- **Evidence after fix:** terminal output from the patched registration pattern:

  ```console
  $ bash /tmp/prove-after.sh
  created temp dir: /var/folders/.../T/tmp.GaAkuJenu8
  TMPFILES=/var/folders/.../T/tmp.GaAkuJenu8
  exists before fail? yes
  simulating fail/exit 1...
  AFTER_PATCH: cleaned path=/var/folders/.../T/tmp.GaAkuJenu8
  ```

  Bare mktemp without trap still leaks (control):

  ```console
  $ bash /tmp/prove-before.sh
  created temp dir: /var/folders/.../T/tmp.NoQGp8tzgN
  simulating fail/exit 1...
  BEFORE_PATCH: LEAKED path=/var/folders/.../T/tmp.NoQGp8tzgN
  ```

- **Observed result after fix:** EXIT trap removes registered temp paths after simulated install fail (`exit 1`). Unregistered bare mktemp still leaks. `bash -n` and shellcheck pass on the production script.
- **What was not tested:** full end-to-end `curl | bash` install-cli run against a live Node download fail injection on CI runners.

## Related

- Pattern already used in `scripts/install.sh` (TMPFILES / trap; direct `TMPFILES+=` for some paths)
- Similar class: temp dir cleanup on every exit path elsewhere in the monorepo

target.title: fix: preserve tools when local-model lean agents use provider overrides
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes local-model lean tool filtering when an agent configured for a local model is temporarily routed to a hosted provider override.

A hosted override must keep the normal tool surface, while local providers and custom local OpenAI-compatible endpoints must retain lean filtering.

## Problem

`experimental.localModelLean=true` was resolved from agent configuration without enough runtime model context. A local-model-oriented agent routed to `meta/muse-spark-1.1` could therefore inherit lean Tool Search behavior and lose the expected direct `exec` surface.

An earlier revision attempted to solve this with a fixed local-provider allowlist. That was too narrow and broke established embedded-runner behavior plus arbitrary custom local providers.

## Implementation

The current implementation resolves locality in this order:

1. A configured provider `localService` is local.
2. A configured model or provider endpoint is classified from its URL.
   - loopback, private IP, local hostname, Docker host aliases, `.local`, `.lan`, and `.home.arpa` are local
   - a public HTTP or HTTPS endpoint is hosted
3. Known local providers and local APIs remain lean eligible.
4. A known hosted provider disables lean mode only when it differs from the agent's configured primary provider.
5. When configuration does not establish an override or endpoint locality, the existing explicit opt-in behavior is preserved.

This avoids treating a generic OpenAI-compatible transport as proof that a model is local or hosted.

## Compatibility

The patch preserves:

- existing config-only lean behavior
- embedded-runner Tool Search defaults
- message-tool-only filtering
- Ollama, llama.cpp, and LM Studio eligibility
- arbitrary custom local OpenAI-compatible providers
- configured local services and private endpoints

It prevents lean mode from applying to hosted provider overrides such as a local agent temporarily routed to Meta.

## Regression Coverage

Coverage includes:

- local primary model to known hosted provider override
- hosted provider selection without a configured override
- arbitrary custom provider on a private endpoint
- custom provider on a public endpoint
- LM Studio provider resolution
- unknown provider fallback behavior
- config-only fallback behavior
- harness tool-surface behavior for hosted and local providers
- existing embedded-runner lean Tool Search and message-tool-only tests

## Validation

Current head: `3de24ad9ea62243fd905f7bb9b897be118f8b0fa`

GitHub Actions passed on the current head:

- CI
- Workflow Sanity
- OpenGrep PR Diff
- CodeQL
- CodeQL Critical Quality
- iOS Periphery Dead Code

## Runtime Evidence

Before the patch:

- `main.experimental.localModelLean=true`
- fresh `main` session
- override: `meta/muse-spark-1.1`
- observed result: `Tool exec not found`

Isolation check before implementation:

- disabling `main.experimental.localModelLean`
- restarting the gateway
- repeating the same fresh Meta smoke
- observed output: `main-meta-fixed-tool-ok`

Current-head automated validation is green. A redacted current-head live hosted-override and local-provider run is still pending because this GitHub repair environment does not have access to the user's provider sessions or local gateway.

## Scope

This PR changes local-model lean runtime scoping only. It does not change configured tool policy, authorization, static provider catalog metadata, or PR #103051.

## Tests

AI-assisted: yes.

target.title: feat(ui): sessions sidebar redesign with agent sections, smart groups, and draft sessions
target.body:
Related: #103431
Stacked on #103432 (protocol/server foundation).

## What Problem This Solves

The sessions sidebar mixed three create affordances (New session, a git-branch worktree button, and a New group prompt), hid agent switching in a compact `<select>` that teleported navigation on change, and rendered channel-originated sessions in one flat list with raw peer ids ("Telegram · 491234567890") and token names ("slack:g-general"). Custom group names/order lived in browser localStorage, so they never followed the operator across devices. Worktree sessions were indistinguishable from plain chats, and there was no way to pick a branch, folder, or node when starting work.

## Why This Change Was Made

Agents are now collapsible top-level sidebar sections: expanding an agent browses its sessions (scoped list fetch, cached per agent) without navigating away from the open chat, and collapsed agents show an unread indicator; single-agent installs keep the flat list. Within an agent, rows classify into built-in smart sections — one per channel (rows keep their human chat titles), a Work section for worktree/exec-node sessions with a `repo ⎇ branch` (plus node) subtitle — followed by custom groups and Chats; an explicit user category always beats smart classification. Naming never falls back to raw keys: DM fallbacks shorten peer ids, dashboard sessions read "New session" until their generated title lands, and unnamed work sessions read as their checkout. The three create buttons collapse into one + that opens a draft dialog (agent, exec host from paired `system.run` nodes, folder, worktree toggle with a `worktrees.branches`-backed base-branch picker and optional name); the first message creates the session and starts the run in a single `sessions.create` call, so abandoned drafts leave nothing behind. The custom group catalog moves onto the gateway (`sessions.groups.*`) with a one-time localStorage migration; rename/delete now update member sessions server-side, deleting the old client-side paging loop.

## User Impact

Multi-agent operators see every agent in the sidebar and can browse one without losing their place. Telegram/Slack/WhatsApp sessions group under their channels with real names; work sessions surface their branch at a glance. Starting a session on a specific branch, folder, or node is a first-class flow. Custom groups follow you across browsers. Plain New Chat semantics (`/new`, main-session reset) are unchanged.

## Evidence

- Live end-to-end on a scratch gateway (isolated `OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR`, two agents, seeded Telegram/Slack/WhatsApp sessions): sidebar rendered agent sections `Main`/`Work agent`, channel groups with titles "Acme #general", "Peter Steinberger", "OpenClaw Devs", "WhatsApp · …345678"; the + dialog listed branches `main/feature-base/topic-x` from `worktrees.branches`, and submitting with base `feature-base` + name `live-test` created branch `openclaw/live-test`, checked out the worktree under the state dir, navigated to the new session, and listed it under **Work** with subtitle `workspace-main ⎇ live-test`. Agent expansion switched session lists without changing the URL; zero console errors.
- `pnpm test ui/src/lib/sessions ui/src/lib/session-display.test.ts ui/src/components/app-sidebar.test.ts ui/src/components/new-session-dialog.test.ts ui/src/lib/agents/index.test.ts` — green, including new coverage for smart-section classification, channel-session detection, name fallbacks, and draft→create param mapping.
- Full `ui/src/pages/sessions`, `ui/src/components`, chat page/pane sweep: green except `lobster-pet`/`lobster-dex`, which fail identically on the base branch (pre-existing, unrelated).
- `pnpm ui:build` clean; `env -u OPENAI_API_KEY pnpm ui:i18n:check` clean (locale bundles regenerated raw-copy, matching the secretless CI lane); tsgo core + test lanes green.

target.title: feat(mobile): share native protocol helpers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Android and Apple maintained separate implementations for Talk directives, device-auth payloads, Bonjour decoding, and gateway custom-header validation. Those implementations had begun to diverge while the native UIs were otherwise independent.

## Why This Change Was Made

This first migration slice introduces a Kotlin Multiplatform core for those protocol helpers. Android retains source-compatible adapters; the shared Apple package provides the stable Swift-facing boundary and hides generated Kotlin types from app callers. The build prepares one Apple XCFramework before SwiftPM and Xcode resolution, covering iOS, watchOS, and macOS consumers.

## User Impact

No UI, storage, transport, or public product behavior is intentionally changed. Existing platform-specific compatibility policies are explicit at the shared boundary, including Bonjour escape decoding, header-value validation, and Talk parsing differences.

## Evidence

- Production diff: 587 additions, 588 deletions.

target.title: fix(gateway): add separate inline avatar size cap for agents.list projection
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where `agents.list` returns oversized inline avatar data URLs, causing multi-megabyte RPC responses that can exceed client timeouts.

`listAgentsForGateway` reads each configured local avatar in full and base64-encodes it into the response with a per‑avatar cap of 2 MB (`AVATAR_MAX_BYTES`). Images carrying embedded metadata—such as C2PA provenance manifests—can easily approach that cap. With three such avatars the observed response was **4.15 MB**, which exceeded Android's default 15‑second request timeout and left the agent list empty on slow links. Issue #103265 reports the root cause; PR #103248 mitigates the Android timeout but does not address the gateway payload.

## Why This Change Was Made

The 2 MB acceptance limit (`AVATAR_MAX_BYTES`) is shared by local file validation, Control UI uploads, and gateway projection. Lowering it would break existing avatar storage for files between 256 KB and 2 MB that users have already configured and uploaded. That is a compatibility change that belongs in a separate maintainer-driven decision, not a bugfix.

Instead, this PR introduces a separate **256 KB inline projection limit** (`AVATAR_INLINE_MAX_BYTES`) that applies only to the agent‑list projection path (`resolveAgentAvatarUrlFromSource`). The shared file opener and data‑URL reader retain the original 2 MB limit, so dedicated avatar delivery via `assistant-avatar.ts` (Control UI, route delivery) is unaffected.

The 256 KB threshold matches the existing `GITHUB_AVATAR_MAX_BYTES` constant, keeping the two external avatar sources at the same inline budget.

**Key design decisions:**

- **Cap placement**: `AVATAR_INLINE_MAX_BYTES` is checked in `resolveAgentAvatarUrlFromSource` after opening the file descriptor. If the file exceeds the inline limit, the descriptor is closed and `undefined` is returned (avatar omitted, no error). A deduplicated `logWarn` fires once per file path.
- **Shared infrastructure preserved**: `openResolvedLocalAgentAvatarFile` and `readOpenedLocalAgentAvatarDataUrl` remain at `AVATAR_MAX_BYTES` (2 MB). They are used by `assistant-avatar.ts` for dedicated avatar delivery and must not be capped.
- **Warning deduplication**: A module‑level `Set<string>` tracks warned file paths so that multiple projections (agents RPC, chat bootstrap, usage aggregation) do not repeat the same warning.
- **Constant location**: `AVATAR_INLINE_MAX_BYTES` lives in `src/shared/avatar-limits.ts` alongside `AVATAR_MAX_BYTES`. It is re‑exported through `src/shared/avatar-policy.ts` for existing importers.

**Files changed (5 files, +179/−3):**

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `src/shared/avatar-limits.ts` | +6: added `AVATAR_INLINE_MAX_BYTES = 256 * 1024` |
| `src/shared/avatar-policy.ts` | +6/−3: re‑export `AVATAR_INLINE_MAX_BYTES` |
| `src/agents/identity-avatar-file.ts` | +28/−3: inline cap in `resolveAgentAvatarUrlFromSource` with deduplicated warning; imports `logWarn` and `AVATAR_INLINE_MAX_BYTES` |
| `src/agents/identity-avatar-file.test.ts` | +59/−1: three new tests for inline cap behavior + `listAgentsForGateway` production proof |
| `src/gateway/proof-avatar-cap.server.test.ts` | +83: real gateway WebSocket RPC proof test |

## User Impact

**End users:** No visible change for most users. Avatar files under 256 KB continue to work exactly as before—they are projected as data‑URLs in `agents.list` and elsewhere.

**Users with avatar files between 256 KB and 2 MB:** Those avatars will no longer appear in `agents.list` responses (the `avatarUrl` key will be `undefined`). The avatars remain accepted and stored on disk; upload behavior is unchanged. The agent's `avatar` config field is still present, so the file is not lost—it is simply not inlined into gateway RPC payloads. A `logWarn` is emitted once per file so operators can identify which agents are affected.

**Plugin and Control UI consumers:** The dedicated avatar delivery path (`assistant-avatar.ts`, `openGatewayAssistantAvatar`) is completely unaffected. Avatars served through the Control UI or route delivery retain the full 2 MB acceptance limit.

**Operators:** `agents.list` payloads are bounded to a predictable size regardless of avatar file sizes, eliminating the Android timeout scenario reported in #103265.

## Evidence

### 1. Production path proof (listAgentsForGateway)

Reproduces the exact function chain used by the `agents.list` and `chat.startup` RPC handlers:

**Three agents with 1.4 MB avatars each** (reproducing the #103265 scenario):

```
3× 1.4 MB avatars payload: 1,456 bytes
```

All three avatars accepted (`avatar` field present), none projected (`avatarUrl: undefined`). Without the cap this would be ~6 MB. With the cap the payload stays under 2 KB.

**Three agents with graduated sizes** (32 KB, 200 KB, 500 KB):

| Avatar | Size | Status | Result |
|--------|------|--------|--------|
| `small.png` | 32 KB (below both limits) | Projected | `data:image/png;base64,…` (43,686 chars) |
| `medium.png` | 200 KB (below inline cap) | Projected | `data:image/png;base64,…` (273,066 chars) |
| `large.png` | 500 KB (between inline cap and acceptance cap) | **Capped** | `avatarUrl: undefined` |

### 2. Real gateway RPC proof

Starts a real gateway via `createGatewaySuiteHarness`, opens a WebSocket, authenticates with `operator.read` scope, and calls `chat.startup` (which includes `agentsList` via the same `listAgentsForGateway` production path).

**Test file:** `src/gateway/proof-avatar-cap.server.test.ts`

```bash
pnpm test src/gateway/proof-avatar-cap.server.test.ts
```
```
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
     Tests  2 passed (2)
```

Runtime output confirmed: `agent-3` (500 KB avatar) returns `avatarUrl: undefined`; agents 1 and 2 return valid data URLs.

### 3. Full test suite

```bash
pnpm test src/agents/identity-avatar-file.test.ts
```
```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  8 passed (8)
```

```bash
pnpm test src/agents/identity-avatar.test.ts
```
```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
     Tests  14 passed (14)
```

All existing avatar resolution, workspace containment, public redaction, and boundary‑escape tests continue to pass with no regression.

### 4. Compatibility verified

- `resolveLocalAgentAvatarPath` acceptance check at `AVATAR_MAX_BYTES` (2 MB) — unchanged
- `openResolvedLocalAgentAvatarFile` file‑open limit at `AVATAR_MAX_BYTES` (2 MB) — unchanged
- `readOpenedLocalAgentAvatarDataUrl` read limit at `AVATAR_MAX_BYTES` (2 MB) — unchanged
- `assistant-avatar.ts` dedicated delivery path — unaffected
- Control UI upload validation — unaffected
- Inline cap at `resolveAgentAvatarUrlFromSource` (256 KB) — only agent‑list projections
- Warning deduplication — each oversized file warned at most once

## Compatibility / Migration

- **Upload and storage limit**: unchanged at 2 MB (`AVATAR_MAX_BYTES`)
- **Inline projection cap**: new at 256 KB (`AVATAR_INLINE_MAX_BYTES`), only in `resolveAgentAvatarUrlFromSource`
- **Dedicated avatar delivery** (Control UI, route delivery): unaffected at 2 MB
- Avatars between 256 KB and 2 MB: remain accepted and stored; `avatarUrl` is `undefined` in agent‑list RPC responses
- No config, environment, or migration changes needed

target.title: fix(acpx): keep Codex wrapper error tail truncation UTF-16 safe
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`readCodexWrapperStderrTail()` uses `text.slice(-6000)` for tail truncation. When a surrogate pair spans the 6000-char tail boundary, the result starts with an orphan low surrogate (`\ude80`) producing `�`.

**Proof on main:**
```js
const input = "🚀" + "x".repeat(5999);   // length 6001
input.slice(-6000)[0] === "\ude80"          // → true, orphan low surrogate
```

## Why This Change Was Made

1. Extracted `tailCodexWrapperError()` helper using `sliceUtf16Safe(text, -6000)`
2. Added 3 test cases including surrogate-pair boundary proof

## User Impact

- Codex wrapper error diagnostics in ACPX keep emoji intact
- No behavior change for ASCII text

## Evidence

- `tailCodexWrapperError` exported and tested directly
- Boundary test constructs input where `slice(-6000)` on main produces a broken low surrogate; fix verifies first code point is never a low surrogate

target.title: fix(browser): respect --timeout-ms for browser evaluate command
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Issue #103137 reports that `openclaw browser evaluate --fn "() => 1 + 1" --timeout-ms 60000` aborts after ~15 seconds, ignoring `--timeout-ms`. Long-running JavaScript evaluations on a live browser session cannot complete.

## Root Cause

The timeout is enforced by the gateway WS runtime (`server/ws-connection.ts:333-349`). It reads `preauthHandshakeTimeoutMs` from the client options, then passes it through `resolvePreauthHandshakeTimeoutMs()` from `packages/gateway-client/src/timeouts.ts`. When that value is `undefined`, the default is `DEFAULT_PREAUTH_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS = 15_000`.

The bug was in `src/gateway/call.ts:callGatewayWithScopes()`: `preauthHandshakeTimeoutMs` was set to only `context.config.gateway?.handshakeTimeoutMs`. When that config key was unset (the common case for users who don't configure gateway handshake timeout), the value was `undefined`, and the runtime fell back to the 15s default — regardless of `--timeout-ms`.

## Fix

```diff
-    preauthHandshakeTimeoutMs: context.config.gateway?.handshakeTimeoutMs,
+    preauthHandshakeTimeoutMs:
+      context.config.gateway?.handshakeTimeoutMs !== undefined
+        ? context.config.gateway.handshakeTimeoutMs
+        : timeoutMs ?? undefined,
```

When `gateway.handshakeTimeoutMs` is not configured, `preauthHandshakeTimeoutMs` now falls back to the request `timeoutMs`, which originates from the user's `--timeout-ms` flag.

## Evidence

### Gateway WS runtime timeout resolution log

The following output traces the actual production code path — from `call.ts` through `createGatewayClient({ preauthHandshakeTimeoutMs })` to `server/ws-connection.ts`:

```
=== Gateway WS runtime: preauth handshake timeout resolution ===
Production code path:
  src/gateway/call.ts - callGatewayWithScopes ->
  createGatewayClient({ preauthHandshakeTimeoutMs }) ->
  server/ws-connection.ts - resolvePreauthHandshakeTimeoutMs() ->
  setTimeout(timer, handshakeTimeoutMs)

DEFAULT_PREAUTH_HANDSHAKE_TIMEOUT_MS = 15000ms (hardcoded)

[BEFORE FIX] user runs with --timeout-ms 60000
  gateway.handshakeTimeoutMs = undefined (common case)
  preauthHandshakeTimeoutMs = undefined
  > resolvePreauthHandshakeTimeoutMs(undefined)
  > returns 15000ms
  > setTimeout(timer, 15000)  ← ABORTS at ~15s, --timeout-ms ignored!

[AFTER FIX]  user runs with --timeout-ms 60000
  gateway.handshakeTimeoutMs = undefined
  preauthHandshakeTimeoutMs = timeoutMs = 60000
  > resolvePreauthHandshakeTimeoutMs(60000)
  > returns 60000ms
  > setTimeout(timer, 60000)  ← --timeout-ms respected!

[EDGE] user configured handshakeTimeoutMs=30000
  gateway.handshakeTimeoutMs = 30000 (explicit)
  preauthHandshakeTimeoutMs = 30000 (handshake always wins)
  > resolvePreauthHandshakeTimeoutMs(30000)
  > returns 30000ms
  > setTimeout(timer, 30000)  ← handshake timeout preserved
```

### Actual gateway production log format when timeout fires (ws-connection.ts:344)
```
[warn] handshake timeout conn=abc peer=wss://127.0.0.1:18789 remote=127.0.0.1:54321 phase=pre-auth
```

target.title: fix(discord): retry reply session init conflicts to prevent silent message loss
target.body:
Closes #102381

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Discord inbound messages could be silently dropped when a reply session initialization conflict (`reply session initialization conflicted for <sessionKey>`) raced with another turn finishing or another event initializing the same session. Telegram, Signal, and Slack already retry this transient condition; Discord did not, so the user saw no reply and the message was lost.

## Why This Change Was Made

Added bounded exponential backoff retry inside `processDiscordMessageInner` (`extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.ts`) to match the existing Telegram callback-submit pattern and Slack/Signal retry semantics. The retry only applies to the specific reply-session-init-conflict error string; all other errors fail fast on the first attempt. If the run is aborted while retrying, the loop stops cleanly and returns without throwing.

**ClawSweeper review follow-up:** the retry boundary was narrowed so context/history preparation runs exactly once and only the dispatch/session-init attempt is retried. This prevents a Discord room event from being recorded twice when a conflict happens.

## User Impact

Discord users are far less likely to see a missing reply after sending a message that races with a session teardown or concurrent turn. Operators no longer need to ask the user to re-send; the retry covers the brief window where the session store CAS conflict occurs.

## Evidence

- Added a focused regression test suite in `extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.test.ts`:
  - retries with exponential backoff until dispatch succeeds (250 ms, 1000 ms, 2500 ms)
  - throws the last error after exhausting retries
  - does not retry unrelated dispatch errors
  - stops retrying when the abort signal fires
  - **records room event history exactly once across conflict retries** (new regression test for the narrowed boundary)
- Full local focused run:
  - `npx vitest run extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.test.ts --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-discord.config.ts` → 120 passed
  - `npx vitest run extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.queue.test.ts --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-discord.config.ts` → 22 passed
  - `npx vitest run extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.test.ts extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.process.abort-skip.test.ts extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.queue.test.ts extensions/discord/src/monitor/message-handler.preflight.test.ts --config test/vitest/vitest.extension-discord.config.ts` → 198 passed
- `oxlint` and `oxfmt` clean on changed files.

## Real behavior proof

This environment does not have the `crabbox` binary or a live Discord bot token, so a redacted live Discord conflict-to-success trace cannot be generated locally. Requesting maintainer help to run the Discord live transport / QA Lab proof on Crabbox, or a maintainer can trigger `@clawsweeper re-review` if the current in-process test evidence is sufficient.

target.title: fix(google-meet): actually leave the Meet call in the browser on leave (#103386)
target.body:
## Summary

Fixes #103386.

`openclaw googlemeet leave <session-id>` on the Chrome transports printed `left <session-id>` and marked the session `ended`, but only ran the registered stop hook (the realtime audio bridge; in transcribe mode nothing at all). No code path touched the meeting, so the browser participant kept sitting in the call — a ghost participant receiving audio/captions after the operator was told it left. Twilio sessions already end the real call via their stop hook, so the transports were inconsistent.

### Change

- `extensions/google-meet/src/transports/types.ts` + `chrome.ts`: join now persists the exact tab identity on the session — `browserTargetId` plus `browserTabOpenedByPlugin` (opened via `/tabs/open` vs adopted via `reuseExistingTab`). `openMeetWithBrowserRequest` returns it through both the local and node launch paths.
- `chrome.ts`: new `leaveChromeMeet` / `leaveChromeMeetOnNode` (shared `leaveMeetWithBrowserRequest` core). Leave acts on the persisted target only: verifies the tab still exists (already-closed is a clean no-op), clicks Meet's **Leave call** button via browser evaluate (reliable now that tabs are pinned to `?hl=en`), then closes the tab **only when the plugin opened it** — reused user-owned tabs get the click but stay open. Failures degrade to session notes instead of throwing.
- `extensions/google-meet/src/runtime.ts`: `leave()` calls the browser leave for `chrome`/`chrome-node` sessions and records the outcome in session notes. Guards:
  - sessions with no tracked tab (e.g. `chrome.launch: false`, or browser control never returned a targetId) get an explicit note instead of a guessy URL match;
  - the internal tab-reassignment path in `join()` passes `keepBrowserTab: true` so agent handoff keeps the in-call tab and avoids lobby re-admission;
  - the shared-tab guard compares the persisted `browserTargetId` + node context — same meeting URL in a different browser/node no longer suppresses departure.
- `docs/plugins/google-meet.md`: `leave` row now documents the Chrome-transport behavior.

### Review follow-up (b95168f8ece)

All three ClawSweeper P1 findings addressed: leave no longer rediscovers tabs by URL (persisted `targetId` from join), never closes tabs it did not open (opened-vs-reused ownership tracked), and the shared-tab guard is scoped to the actual target + browser context. A reused-tab regression test now covers the default `reuseExistingTab: true` path end to end.

## Verification

- `pnpm test extensions/google-meet` — 17 files, 209 tests passed. New/updated regressions: plugin-opened tab leave (click + close on the exact persisted target), reused user-owned tab leave (click, `DELETE` throws in the mock if attempted, tab stays open), already-closed tab leave (clean note, no `DELETE`), and a vm test that the leave script clicks only an enabled Leave call button.
- `pnpm tsgo:extensions && pnpm tsgo:extensions:test` — clean.
- oxfmt / oxlint on touched files — clean.

## Real behavior proof

Behavior addressed: `googlemeet leave` leaves the browser participant in the Google Meet call on chrome/chrome-node transports while reporting `left`.
Real environment tested: No live Google Meet call was run; behavior is proven at the browser-proxy request boundary with the plugin's existing stubbed-gateway test harness (same harness the join/status paths use), covering opened, reused, and already-closed tab lifecycles.
Exact steps or command run after this patch: `pnpm test extensions/google-meet` and `pnpm test extensions/google-meet/index.test.ts`.
Evidence after fix: "leaves the Meet call in the browser when a chrome session leaves" asserts the `/act` evaluate carries the leave-click script against the persisted join target and that `DELETE /tabs/local-meet-tab` is issued; "keeps a reused Meet tab open on leave" asserts the same click against an adopted pre-existing tab with a mock that throws on any `DELETE`.
Observed result after fix: 209/209 tests pass; leave issues real browser actions scoped to the session's own tab and records an explanatory note in every fallback path.
What was not tested: A live Meet meeting (real Chrome, real Google account) and the chrome-node transport against a physical node; both share `leaveMeetWithBrowserRequest`, which is covered by the harness. Live-call proof of actual participant departure is pending a real Meet setup.

target.title: ci(release): add plugin npm artifact preflight
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Release operators could not prove the exact npm package bytes for a selected official plugin without entering the plugin publication workflow's approval, credential, OIDC, or mutation paths.

## Why This Change Was Made

This adds an explicit `preflight_only` route to the trusted-main Plugin NPM Release workflow. It validates exact main/release target ancestry before running any target-local setup action or dependency command, packs every selected publishable package including an already-published version, uploads an immutable staging artifact, and independently reads it back against the exact target Git source.

The staging `plugin-npm-package-source-<sourceSha>-<extensionId>` artifact contains the tarball, npm pack metadata, and readback manifest. The final consumer artifact `plugin-npm-package-<extensionId>-<version>` contains the tarball plus `openclaw.plugin-npm-package-evidence/v2`. Its `publicationArtifact` tuple binds the staging artifact id, name, digest, exact target `package.json` hash, packed `package.json` hash, and tarball hash. The evidence also records the publication route, workflow SHA, run attempt, and target SHA. Source and packed hashes are independently recomputed before evidence is written.

The registry readback distinguishes complete publication, mirror-only drift, and stale primary `beta`, `alpha`, or `latest` tags (`npm-tag-repair`). The route is structurally isolated from release approval, the `npm-release` environment, secrets, OIDC, npm publish/dist-tag changes, ClawHub, and native publication jobs.

## User Impact

Release maintainers can validate exact plugin package bytes for a main or release target SHA without publishing or mutating registry state. Existing Tideclaw publication behavior is unchanged and is not advertised as supported by this preflight contract. There is no end-user runtime behavior change.

## Evidence

- Previous exact-head Blacksmith Testbox baseline: 250/250 tests passed across the plugin workflow contract and changed-test routing (`29101795446`, job `86392276200`).
- Focused Testbox proof: 30/30 tests passed on equivalent head `531384a45ae22159432e667099d87891c1583436` using `tbx_01kx6b3hrsdn93dp41t6hffx8x` (`29104673836`).
